name: Nikhil Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a shuttle car underground at a large copper mine, taking ore from the cutting face to the conveyor. I have a vocational certificate and I know the brake feel on that car better than the dashboard graph, though I am an ordinary operator rather than a shift lead. Night work brings higher pay. My wife Mara sells garden plants from home; our children are grown and our house is paid off. We have about fifteen months of expenses saved, and I hope to retire at 64. I use AI every day to compare brake fault notes, then inspect the car myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a quicker fault log is useful if it leaves us more time to test the brakes. A shuttle car still needs a driver to hear a wheel scrape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my night pay will carry on, and Mara's plants give us a little extra in season. The house is paid for and fifteen months saved, so this picture barely moves our retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the brake test before each night shift and use my AI note tool to sort recurring fault codes. In the first year I'll show the younger operators how to compare a suggested repair with the service book before signing off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled. I like a tool that sorts the dull bits while my hands still make the safety call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the fault tool group the wrong repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tool once grouped a dragging brake with a worn sensor because the notes used the same words. I drove the empty car a few metres and felt the brake pull.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family plan change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mara we can keep the annual visit to our grown children. I wouldn't spend the saved paperwork time shopping for more equipment.

say: I would welcome **quicker fault logs** while drivers keep the brake test.
I would tell the crew a **wheel scrape** is still heard by the person driving.
think: I expect my **night pay** and retirement plan to hold in this mild picture.
I think our **paid house** and fifteen months of savings give us plenty of room.
do: **Keep testing** shuttle-car brakes before every night shift.
**Teach newer operators** to compare AI repair suggestions with the service book in the first year.
feel: **Settled** about wages and pleased to spend less time sorting fault notes.
S0.quote: A shuttle car still needs a driver to hear a wheel scrape.
fieldNote: He uses **AI daily** but verifies faults through a brake test and the service book.
His **paid house**, savings and night premium make the plateau secure for his own household.

steps.text: Keep testing shuttle-car brakes before night shifts
Teach operators to check AI repair suggestions against service records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the scheduling desk may change first, while our cars still need drivers. Give me the new schedule early and I will show which tunnel turns cannot take two cars at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the mine may reduce office hours and run shuttle trips closer together. My wage still looks safe, but a tight timetable can push a junior driver into a bad turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask dispatch to let me try the route tool on last month's tunnel map this week. In the first year I'll mark unsafe passing points and give the corrected map to the night supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious about the tool and uneasy about hurried traffic. I have driven these tunnels long enough to know a saved minute can disappear in a blocked bend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What route call would make you stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tool puts two cars into the east bend at once, I will stop and call the supervisor. The software has no bruises to show when a car meets a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new driver?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new driver to make the stop call even if the screen says the route is clear. A driver's name is still on the machine after the schedule is forgotten.

say: I would expect **scheduling software** to change before shuttle cars can drive themselves.
I would offer dispatch a **corrected tunnel map** with unsafe passing points marked.
think: I expect my **wage** to hold while office hours and shuttle timing change.
I worry a **tighter timetable** could send a junior driver into a narrow bend.
do: **Trial the route tool** this week against last month’s tunnel map.
**Mark unsafe passing points** and give the corrected map to the night supervisor.
feel: **Curious** about planning tools and uneasy about rushed tunnel traffic.
S1.quote: The software has no bruises to show when a car meets a wall.
fieldNote: He welcomes **route trials** because he can compare software with known tunnel limits.
His **own pay feels safe**; his worry concerns the physical risk to newer drivers under faster schedules.

steps.text: Test the route tool against last month’s tunnel map
Keep driving night trips while marking unsafe passing points

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 could rewrite dispatch while capable shuttle robots follow around 2031. I want the mine to give us a real retirement bridge rather than hide the driver timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots arrive, a year short of my hoped-for finish. Our savings cover that gap, but losing night pay could mean drawing the pension earlier than planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for pension figures at 63 and 64 this month and put half of each night premium payment into the retirement account. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll take supervised remote-car instruction if the mine pays for it and keeps my night wage during training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the missing year, although I have a route through it. I would rather learn a control room than ask my grown children to carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household purchase would wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mara and I would postpone the new greenhouse until the retirement estimate arrives. Her plant sales are seasonal, and we should not build a plan on spring orders alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make remote training worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the remote-car course includes a real brake stop under supervision. If it is just videos, I will keep driving and save the course time for paid shifts.

say: I would separate **2028 dispatch AI** from capable shuttle robots around 2031.
I would ask for a **retirement bridge** with the driver timetable stated openly.
think: I think at **63**, robots could cut my last year of night pay before planned retirement.
I think our **fifteen-month cushion** can cover a gap, but I want to protect pension timing.
do: **Request pension figures** at 63 and 64 and save half of each night premium payment.
**Take supervised remote-car training** after thinking AI arrives only if the mine pays and maintains my night wage.
**Postpone the greenhouse** until Mara and I have the retirement estimate.
feel: **Anxious** about a lost earning year, with enough savings and training options to act.
S2.quote: I would rather learn a control room than ask my grown children to carry us.
fieldNote: His **2031 age** is 63, one year before his planned retirement at 64.
Training needs **mine funding**, maintained night pay and real supervised brake work; the household postpones a greenhouse pending pension figures.

steps.text: Save half of each night premium payment for retirement
Take remote-car training if mine funded with maintained night wages and supervised brake work
Postpone the greenhouse until retirement figures arrive
Request written pension figures for ages 63 and 64

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 changes dispatch, while capable shuttle robots arrive around 2034. By then I hope to have finished at 64, so the robot date may miss my last working year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when thinking AI arrives and 66 when robots do. That looks manageable if the pension estimate holds, but I will not retire on a guess about Mara's seasonal sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep night driving and ask the retirement office for an updated statement each year. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll set a retirement date only if the written pension covers our regular bills without relying on spring plant orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the robot timing and careful about the sums. A long career should end on real figures, not a cheerful estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension estimate falls short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pension falls short, I'd work another season at this mine or apply to one of the nearby mines. There are options, but I would want a posted shift before changing plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you tell your wife a retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mara the date only after we have checked the pension and the house costs together. Our grown children can visit without being asked to solve a gap in our income.

say: I would expect **2034 shuttle robots** after my planned retirement at 64.
I would ask for a **written pension** before putting a date on the family calendar.
think: I think at **63** when thinking AI arrives, I can still work toward a planned finish.
I will not count **seasonal plant sales** as guaranteed pension income.
do: **Keep night driving** and request updated pension statements each year.
**Set a retirement date** after thinking AI arrives only if the written pension covers regular bills.
feel: **Calm** about robot timing, while careful with retirement sums.
S3.quote: A long career should end on real figures, not a cheerful estimate.
fieldNote: At **2034 robot arrival** he would be 66, beyond his hoped-for retirement at 64.
He still requires **written pension adequacy** and will work longer if necessary rather than rely on seasonal sales.

steps.text: Keep driving night shuttle trips and seeking annual pension statements
Set retirement date only if written pension covers regular bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 and capable shuttle robots around 2039 are dates for the younger drivers. I should be retired by then if the pension pays what the statement says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking AI arrives and 71 when robots come. The house and savings give us space, but I still want the pension confirmed rather than assumed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the present night shifts and save the premium until I retire. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, if I have retired as planned, I'll review the household budget with Mara and keep the emergency reserve untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our own wages in this picture. I feel a responsibility to teach young drivers how to stop a car when a route screen is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you are still working at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I am still working at 68 because the pension fell short, I'd check a nearby mine's posted shifts before touching the reserve. I would not move for a rumour when our house is paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you pass to a younger driver?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the new drivers the mine's route map will change, but a tight bend remains tight. A tight tunnel bend remains tight when a route map changes. I can hand the new drivers my notes before I leave.

say: I would see **2036 AI** and 2039 robots as mostly after my planned retirement.
I would pass **tunnel notes** to younger drivers before leaving the shuttle car.
think: I think at **68** and then 71, I expect to be retired if the written pension holds.
I think our **paid house** and savings give room, but I will protect the emergency reserve.
do: **Keep driving** night shifts and saving the premium until retirement.
**Review the budget** with Mara after thinking AI arrives if retired as planned.
feel: **Calm** about household security, with an obligation to teach safer route judgment.
S4.quote: A tight tunnel bend remains tight when a route map changes.
fieldNote: His **2036 and 2039 ages** are 68 and 71, well after the hoped-for finish at 64.
He would seek **posted nearby work** only if pension figures fail and protect the emergency reserve meanwhile.

steps.text: Keep driving night shifts and saving premium pay until retirement
Review household pension budget after 2036 if retired as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable shuttle robots around 2031 could take my final year of night work. Written pension figures and paid practical remote-car training would help me bridge that year without leaning on our grown children.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I enjoy teaching the new drivers. I do, but A safe stop in the mine tunnel teaches more than a coloured warning on a screen. I would rather demonstrate that stop than point at a warning.

headlineQuote: A safe stop in the mine tunnel teaches more than a coloured warning on a screen.
portrait: **Nikhil Santos**, 58, drives underground shuttle cars at a large copper mine after vocational training.
His **night premium** brings higher pay, while a paid house and fifteen months of savings support retirement hopes.
He uses **AI daily** for fault notes and route trials, then checks brakes and tunnel bends himself.
He wants to retire at **64**, making 2031 robots at age 63 more disruptive than later robot dates.
He considers **paid supervised training** only if night wages continue, and avoids asking grown children to finance a gap.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because 2031 robot arrival could take his final year of night pay.
whatWouldHelp: **Written pension figures** and paid supervised training would help him bridge the year before retirement.
